item.title: MagTrace: Tracing magnetic order through the evolving scientific literature
item.description: arXiv:2611.28338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Much of the research on magnetic materials starts from their magnetic order, but confirming it from the papers by hand can take hours, and curated databases can be incomplete and outdated. In this work, we build MagTrace, a language model agent that, given only a material's name, searches four literature databases, reads open access full text and reports the magnetic orders the current literature supports, each with a confidence score and citations a reader can check. We evaluate its performance on 18 materials against an answer key complied from published papers, compared with two other conditions that vary in level of retrieval. On a score from 0 to 1 that combines correctness, detail, whether the most confident order is current, and citation integrity, MagTrace scores 0.839; the same underlying language model scores 0.676 given the abstracts from one literature search and 0.548 answering from memory. With a single search, the model finds the right kind of order but omits the propagation vector, which describes how the pattern repeats through the material's crystal structure, in 85% of its orders. From memory, the model often cites titles that lead to no indexed paper (for 25% of the orders we could check), and when a cited paper exists and has an abstract, the abstract contradicts the claim for 17% of those citations, against 7% for MagTrace.
item.dc:creator: Mengnan Sun, Cheng Peng

item.title: Recent Reversal in Single-Authored Papers
item.description: arXiv:2611.30189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The number of authors per scientific paper has risen for decades, and the share of single-authored papers has correspondingly declined, a pattern long documented across fields. This study shows that on arXiv.org this decline has recently reversed. Findings indicate that for submissions between 2015 and early 2026, after falling steadily for a decade, the single-author share rose from 10.9% in 2024 to 11.2% in 2025, and in the first quarter it rose from 10.7% in 2025 to 12.9% in 2026. This is the largest single year-over-year first-quarter change in the studied window, and the first increase in the first-quarter series. In 2025, for the first time in the studied period, the number of single-authored papers grew faster year-over-year than the number of multi-authored papers, reversing the long-standing pattern. This reversal is notable because it is broad, rising within all eight top-level arXiv categories, and because it reflects a genuine change in authoring practice within fields rather than the shifting disciplinary composition of arXiv submissions. A comparison of five arXiv snapshots spanning 2022 to 2026 confirms that the finding is not an artifact of incomplete or revised author metadata in recent submissions. As robustness checks, article-type records from OpenAlex, a database covering a broader range of disciplines, and an arXiv snapshot extended through September 2026 both confirm these findings. This latest snapshot shows the share still rising, to 14.1% in Q2 and 17.0% in Q3 of 2026, compared with 10.5% and 11.1% in the same quarters of 2025.
item.dc:creator: Abdulkareem Alsudais

item.title: CHICO: Bridging Sparse Metadata and Multimodal Evidence in Cultural Heritage Collections
item.description: arXiv:2611.30923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cultural heritage aggregators provide access to millions of digitized items. Yet their catalog records often contain sparse, heterogeneous metadata, with associated media links that may not lead to accessible images. Structuring and validating these resources for multimodal AI research can support reproducible experimentation. To this end, we present CHICO (Cultural Heritage Images and Catalog Objects), a multimodal dataset derived from Europeana that brings together curated catalog fields, images, and contextual information to support evidence-grounded description generation while retaining the original Europeana records. It comprises more than 60,000 cultural heritage records with associated images. Although originally developed for that purpose, it can also support multimodal information retrieval, metadata enrichment, and evidence-based evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Vagner In\'acio de Oliveira, Paula Dornhofer Paro Costa

item.title: A Data-Mining Approach to Library User Segmentation: Clustering Readers by Perceived Marketing Communication
item.description: arXiv:2611.28028v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper applies unsupervised data mining to segment users of information-library centers by their perception of digital and marketing communication. The empirical basis is a survey of readers from fifteen information-library centers in Uzbekistan. From 213 responses, 180 complete records with seven Likert-scale perception variables were retained. After z-score standardization, k-means clustering was used, and the number of clusters was selected by the silhouette coefficient with additional validation by the Calinski-Harabasz and Davies-Bouldin indices. A stable four-cluster solution was obtained: Engaged Enthusiasts, Moderately Satisfied, Loyal-in-spite-of and Disengaged. The main finding is a perception-loyalty paradox: some users remain satisfied even when mediated communication is weakly perceived. The proposed segmentation provides a reproducible instrument for differentiated communication planning in library management.

item.title: Disclosure Bias in AI Reviewers
item.description: arXiv:2611.30410v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI models increasingly help to review papers, and many conferences and journals now require authors to state how they used AI. Does this AI-use statement change how an AI reviewer rates a paper, and could it change which papers are accepted? In a preliminary study, we varied only the AI-use statement of 150 ICLR 2027 submissions, in up to nine versions adapted from real statements: from no AI, through writing help and coding, to an AI research agent and an AI author. Six AI reviewers rated the versions: the decision model Jev and the language models Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 4 Argon. Across 23,652 reviews, we find that every reviewer rates papers lower on average when the statement says AI did all the work than under a statement of no AI use. The AI research agent statement lowers the rating significantly for Jev, Sonnet and Argon. We find no evidence of a disclosure bias for AI assistance: for writing help, coding and research help, no reviewer's rating differs significantly from its rating under a statement of no AI use. Whether the observed penalty changes which papers are accepted depends on more than the size of the penalty: on how finely and how consistently the reviewer separates the papers near the acceptance boundary, on whether the penalty is spread over all papers or concentrated on a few, and possibly on how many other papers disclose AI use.
item.dc:creator: Jens Leysen, Noah Dani\"els, Marco Favier, Bart Goethals

item.title: Survivors in science: A comprehensive analysis of gender disparities
item.description: arXiv:2512.22140v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Gender inequality in scientific careers can emerge at two analytically distinct margins: inequality in who remains in science and inequality among those who remain. While the former has been examined in research on attrition in science, much less is known about gender disparities among scientists who remain active for a long period. We address this gap by following 'survivors in science' - scientists who started publishing in 2000 and continued publishing until 2020-2023 (N = 41,424). Together, they authored more than 2 million publications (N - 2,089,097) containing over 70 million cited references (N - 73,118,395) and worked in 38 OECD countries. Using raw Scopus data, we examine gender disparities in publishing intensity, international collaboration, journal prestige, productivity, citation impact and team size. Our findings reveal that men were on average 23% more productive than women cumulatively in 2000-2023 and 19% more productive in 2019-2023. By contrast, women and men published in similarly prestigious journals, achieved similar field-normalized citation impact, and worked in similarly sized teams. The structure of gender inequality is career-stage dependent: Disparities observed in broader populations of scientists need not persist among those who remain active in science longer, while the gender productivity gap persists.
item.dc:creator: Marek Kwiek, Lukasz Szymula

item.title: LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment
item.description: arXiv:2606.04382v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated subject cataloging assigns controlledvocabulary headings to bibliographic records, but LCSH has no standard public benchmark. We introduce LCSHBench: 22,346 books in 15 languages from the openly licensed Harvard, Columbia, and Princeton catalogs. Records enter only when at least two independent cataloging agencies assigned LCSH; we release per-catalog provenance plus union and unanimous answer views. A concordance study of 465,187 works cataloged by all three libraries shows why this design matters: libraries usually agree on the underlying topic (93.3% share a concept-level heading) but often differ in exact expression (39.4% have identical heading sets). LCSHBench therefore scores both exact and concept matches, with set and rank metrics broken down by language and heading type, across open-vocabulary generation and full-vocabulary retrieval. As a first demonstration, a low-rank fine-tune of a 300M on-device embedder improves cross-lingual retrieval and beats a 3,072-dimensional hosted embedder on development exact recall@200 (0.659 vs 0.623). The language panel shows the gain is not uniform, and held-out-test and end-to-end confirmation remain future work.
item.dc:creator: Kwok Leong Tang

item.title: Invisible to humans, visible to machines: a preregistered audit of Unicode fidelity across four biomedical bibliographic APIs
item.description: arXiv:2606.24897v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: To develop a reusable, preregistered method for auditing the character-level fidelity of bibliographic application programming interfaces (APIs), and to apply it to four public APIs used to build biomedical text corpora. Preregistered audit (OSF osf.io/zjevr). From the 2024 PubMed Central (PMC) Open Access subset, a simple random sample of 4,000 English-language research articles was drawn. Abstracts returned by the PubMed E-utilities, Crossref, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were compared with the PMC Journal Article Tag Suite (JATS) XML abstract for 51 registered code points, 34 of them in four primary classes: typographic punctuation, mathematical/scientific symbols, Greek letters and special whitespace. A cell (API x class) was classified as systematic loss when the upper 95% Wilson bound of conditional preservation was below 5%, and as faithful when the lower bound exceeded 90%. The mechanism of each loss was examined in the aligned text and the raw API responses. Two of 16 cells met the loss criterion. PubMed preserved typographic punctuation in 0.6% of eligible abstracts (12/2,113; 95% CI 0.3-1.0%), replacing it with ASCII equivalents. OpenAlex preserved special whitespace in 0.0% (0/1,085; 95% CI 0.0-0.4%), which its inverted-index format cannot store. Mathematical symbols and Greek letters were preserved by all four APIs (95.2-99.7%). Crossref returned an abstract for 75.4% of papers (95% CI 74.1-76.7%) and for none published by Elsevier (0/360) or the American Chemical Society (0/105). The same published abstract reaches text-mining pipelines with different characters depending on the API that serves it. Studies that analyze characters, including character-level markers of writing assisted by large language models, should take text from a source shown to preserve those characters, or normalize all sources identically, and report the API and retrieval date.
item.dc:creator: Przemys{\l}aw Czuma

item.title: Trajectories and Comparative Analysis of Global Countries Dominating AI Publications, 2000-2025
item.description: arXiv:2509.25298v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study investigates the shifting global dynamics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) research by analysing the trajectories of countries dominating AI publications between 2000 and 2025. Drawing on the OpenAlex datasets and employing fractional counting to avoid double attribution in co-authored work, the research maps the relative shares of AI publications across major global players. The analysis reveals a profound restructuring of the international AI research landscape. The US and the European Union (representing EU27), once the established leaders, have experienced a notable decline in relative dominance, with their combined share of publications falling from over 57% in 2000 to less than 25% in 2025. In contrast, China has undergone a dramatic ascent, expanding its global share of AI publications from under 5% in 2000 to nearly 36% by 2025, emerging as the single most dominant contributor. Alongside China, India has also risen substantially, consolidating a multipolar Asian research ecosystem. These findings raise questions about the strategic implications of concentrated research output, including China's potential capacity to shape the future direction of AI innovation, which publication data alone cannot establish. Beyond publication volume, the study further examines citation impact, treated as a proxy for research influence but not research quality, by comparing each country's share of high-impact publications against its overall output, and analyses citation impact trajectories across major players. The findings show that in addition to China leading in volume, the country has also recently held the largest share of citation-based high-impact publications. Such an observation challenges the assumption that Western powers retain dominance in highly cited AI scholarship, although citation-based indicators cannot by themselves establish differences in research quality.
item.dc:creator: Jason Hung
